title: Polynomial-time constant approximation for the General Scheduling Problem
formal: For the explicitly encoded General Scheduling Problem below, is there a deterministic polynomial-time approximation with a universal constant factor?
definitions: An instance has n jobs, positive integer processing requirements p_j and nonnegative integer release times r_j in binary. Time is divided into unit slots [t,t+1); a job may occupy arbitrary slots at integer t≥r_j, at most one job per slot, until p_j slots have been allocated. Completion time C_j is one plus the last occupied slot. Let H=max_j r_j+∑_j p_j; schedules are required to finish by H. Each cost function f_j:{0,…,H}→Q_≥0 is supplied by a list of integer breakpoints and rational values, encoded in binary, constant between consecutive breakpoints and nondecreasing. Minimize ∑_j f_j(C_j). This is an explicit discrete-time, piecewise-constant input variant; each job may be preempted between slots at no cost. Output is a list of intervals assigned to jobs, not an H-slot expansion. Running time and output length must be polynomial in total binary input length L, even if H is exponential in L. The guarantee is cost≤c OPT for one absolute finite c, including cost zero when OPT=0.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the stated proposition or its negation, for precisely the specified model. A conditional impossibility must state and prove its complexity implication. A quasipolynomial running time or polynomial dependence on numeric H is not the requested bound.
context: The newer constant-factor result is quasipolynomial and imposes a numeric processing-time restriction; neither feature is silently removed here.
why: A constant approximation would unify many completion-time objectives under one general scheduling model.

import_provenance.original_title: Polynomial-time constant approximation for the General Scheduling Problem
import_provenance.original_statement: For preemptive scheduling on one machine, with release times and arbitrary nonnegative nondecreasing job-specific completion-cost functions, is there a polynomial-time constant-factor approximation to the sum of costs? This asks to improve the O(log log P) guarantee of Bansal and Pruhs, where P is the ratio of largest to smallest processing time.
import_provenance.supplied_caveat: Remark: The November 2025 constant-factor result is quasipolynomial-time and assumes quasipolynomially bounded integer processing times; it does not resolve the polynomial-time question.
